title: Data and models
text:
The dataset comes from a French insurer and is published on OpenML in two tables: one row per policy (risk features and exposure) and one row per claim (claim amount). It contains 678,013 policies.







Feature
Description




Area, Region
Where the policyholder lives


Density
Inhabitants per km² in the policyholder’s city


DrivAge
Age of the driver


BonusMalus
Bonus-malus level: below 100 means a claim-free history, above 100 a surcharge


VehPower, VehAge, VehBrand, VehGas
Vehicle power, age, brand and fuel


Exposure
Fraction of a year the policy was in force (≤ 1)





HasClaim (binary). 1 if the policy had at least one claim during its exposure period, 0 otherwise. Only 3.7% of policies had a claim, so the classes are heavily imbalanced, which is typical for real classification problems and important for how metrics behave.
PurePremium (continuous). Total claim cost divided by exposure, i.e. the cost per policy-year. It’s what an insurer has to charge (before expenses) to cover claims. 96.3% of policies have a pure premium of 0, and the rest have a long right tail. Because pure premium is a rate per year, a policy observed for a full year carries more information than one observed for a week. All pure-premium models and metrics are therefore weighted by exposure.






NoteData preparation




The claim count is taken from the claims table, so HasClaim and PurePremium always agree.
Total claim cost per policy is capped at 200,000 EUR (a few claims reach 4 million), and exposure is capped at 1 year.
Average cost per claim (‘severity’) was considered as a target and dropped: in this dataset, no model predicts it better than the overall mean.

pp = policies.loc[policies["PurePremium"] > 0, "PurePremium"]
pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Statistic": ["Policies", "Claim rate", "Share with pure premium 0",
                      "Median pure premium (when > 0)", "99th percentile (when > 0)"],
        "Value": [n_policies, claim_rate, share_zero,
                  f"{pp.median():,.0f} EUR", f"{pp.quantile(0.99):,.0f} EUR"],
    }
)

title: Data and models
text:
California Housing
A classic regression dataset (shipped with scikit-learn): the median house value of 20,640 Californian districts from the 1990 census, in units of 100,000 USD, with 8 features such as median income, house age and location. Unlike pure premium, it has a strong, smooth signal, so we use it to show how error metrics behave in the textbook case. It has one quirk: values were capped at 5.0 when the data was collected, which shows up in the residual plots.

Null is the ‘no model’ reference. Any metric value only means something next to what the Null model achieves.
GLM is the traditional, interpretable baseline, still the standard in insurance pricing. The insurance GLMs use one-hot encoded categoricals, binned vehicle and driver age, and log-scaled density and bonus-malus.
GBM (HistGradientBoosting in scikit-learn) is the flexible challenger. It handles the categorical features natively and stops adding trees when a validation split stops improving.

The models are deliberately reasonable but not heavily tuned: the project is about measuring performance, not maximizing it.

title: ROC curve and AUC
text: Question answered: does the model rank policies with a claim above policies without one?

title: ROC curve and AUC
text:
Every threshold at once
On the previous page, each threshold gave one confusion matrix and with it one pair of rates:

the true positive rate (TPR, recall): the share of claims we flag, and
the false positive rate (FPR): the share of non-claims we flag.

The ROC curve (receiver operating characteristic) plots this pair for every possible threshold. A very high threshold flags nothing: the curve starts at (0, 0). Lowering it flags more and more policies until everything is flagged, at (1, 1). The marked points are the thresholds from the previous page:


Code
ax = plot_roc(y, {"GBM": b["GBM"]},
              operating_points={"t = 0.2": ("GBM", 0.2), "t = 0.1": ("GBM", 0.1), "t = 0.05": ("GBM", 0.05)})








Figure 1: ROC curve of the GBM, with three thresholds marked.





The diagonal is a model that ranks at random: whatever share of policies it flags, it flags the same share of claims and non-claims. The further a curve bulges towards the top-left corner, the better the model ranks.

title: ROC curve and AUC
text:
AUC: two interpretations
The area under the ROC curve (AUC) condenses the curve into one number between 0 and 1. It has two equivalent readings.
1. Geometric. The area under the curve: 1.0 for a perfect model, 0.5 for random ranking (the diagonal).
2. Probabilistic. The AUC is the probability that a randomly chosen policy with a claim gets a higher score than a randomly chosen policy without one (ties count half):
\[
\text{AUC} = P\left(\hat p_i > \hat p_j \mid y_i = 1,\ y_j = 0\right).
\]
The second reading makes clear that AUC measures ranking only. It’s the Mann–Whitney U statistic, and it can be computed from ranks without drawing any curve. On the toy example, 20 of the 4 × 6 = 24 (claim, no-claim) pairs are ordered correctly: 20/24 = 0.833.
On the real test set, both computations agree, and so does a brute-force check that samples random pairs:

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
p_pos = b.loc[y == 1, "GBM"].to_numpy()
p_neg = b.loc[y == 0, "GBM"].to_numpy()
i, j = rng.integers(len(p_pos), size=1_000_000), rng.integers(len(p_neg), size=1_000_000)
sampled = np.mean(p_pos[i] > p_neg[j]) + 0.5 * np.mean(p_pos[i] == p_neg[j])

roc = roc_points(y, b["GBM"])
pd.Series({
    "Area under the curve (trapezoids)": auc_trapezoid(roc["fpr"], roc["tpr"]),
    "Rank statistic (Mann–Whitney)": auc_rank(y, b["GBM"]),
    "1 million random pairs": sampled,
}, name="AUC").round(4).to_frame()

Gini coefficient
Credit scoring and insurance usually report the Gini coefficient (also called the accuracy ratio or Somers’ D) instead:
\[
\text{Gini} = 2 \cdot \text{AUC} - 1.
\]
It rescales AUC so that random ranking scores 0 and perfect ranking scores 1. The GBM’s AUC of 0.713 is a Gini of 0.425. The insurance Gini computed from a Lorenz curve is a close relative.

title: ROC curve and AUC
text:
Comparing the models


Code
ax = plot_roc(y, {m: b[m] for m in ("Null", "GLM", "GBM")})








Figure 3: ROC curves of all three models on the test set.





The Null model gives everyone the same score, so its curve is the diagonal (AUC 0.5). The GBM (AUC 0.713) ranks better than the GLM (AUC 0.694). Its curve lies on or above the GLM’s at 100% of false positive rates. Where one curve lies above another, that model is better at every threshold in that region. When curves cross, AUC alone hides which model is better in the region you actually operate in.
How large is an AUC of 0.71? There is no universal scale. Whether a claim happens depends largely on chance, so even a perfect pricing model would be far from AUC 1. Judge AUC against the Null model, a simpler baseline and what is achievable for the problem, not against an absolute benchmark.

title: ROC curve and AUC
section: What AUC does not tell you
text:
What AUC does not tell you
It ignores calibration. AUC depends only on the order of the predictions. Any transformation that keeps the order leaves it unchanged, even one that ruins the probabilities:

variants = {
    "GBM": b["GBM"],
    "GBM / 10": b["GBM"] / 10,
    "GBM ^ 0.2": b["GBM"] ** 0.2,
}
pd.DataFrame({
    "AUC": {k: auc_rank(y, v) for k, v in variants.items()},
    "Average predicted probability": {k: v.mean() for k, v in variants.items()},
    "Actual claim rate": {k: y.mean() for k in variants},
}).round(3)

All three rank equally well, but only the first predicts claim probabilities that resemble reality. If the probabilities themselves matter (pricing, expected cost, the threshold formula on the previous page), measure calibration as well.
It weighs all thresholds equally. AUC averages over the whole curve, including regions no one would use. With 96% non-claims, a false positive rate of just 10% already means 16,327 false alarms on the test set. If only the top few percent of scores will ever be acted on, look at the left part of the curve, at precision–recall curves, or at lift charts.
It is an estimate. The test set is a sample, so AUC has sampling uncertainty. Before concluding that the GBM beats the GLM, we need a confidence interval for the difference, from a bootstrap or DeLong’s test.

title: ROC curve and AUC
text:
Takeaways

The ROC curve shows the trade-off between catching positives (TPR) and false alarms (FPR) across all thresholds.
AUC is the probability of ranking a random positive above a random negative: 0.5 is random, 1.0 is perfect. Gini = 2·AUC − 1.
AUC measures ranking only: it says nothing about whether the probabilities are right.
Under heavy imbalance, complement it with precision–recall or lift, and always quantify its uncertainty when comparing models.

title: Confusion matrix and threshold metrics
text: Question answered: if we turn the model’s probabilities into yes/no decisions, how good are those decisions?

title: Confusion matrix and threshold metrics
text:
From probabilities to decisions
Our models predict a probability of a claim. Many uses need a decision instead: inspect this policy or not, refer it to underwriting or not. The usual way to get one is to pick a threshold \(t\) and predict
\[
\hat y = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \hat p \ge t \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}
\]
Every metric on this page evaluates the model together with a threshold. Change the threshold and all of them change.

title: Confusion matrix and threshold metrics
text:
The confusion matrix
Comparing decisions with outcomes gives four kinds of cases:









Predicted 0
Predicted 1




Actual 0
true negative (TN)
false positive (FP), ‘false alarm’


Actual 1
false negative (FN), ‘miss’
true positive (TP)



Here is the GBM on the 169,504 test policies at the conventional threshold of 0.5 and at a much lower threshold of 0.05:


Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.8))
plot_confusion_matrix(c_half, ax=axes[0], title="Threshold 0.5")
plot_confusion_matrix(c_low, ax=axes[1], title="Threshold 0.05")
fig.tight_layout()








Figure 1: Confusion matrices of the GBM at two thresholds. Color intensity is on a log scale.





At 0.5, the model flags just 2 policies, and 0 of them had a claim. Its highest predicted probability is only 0.52: with a claim rate of 3.7%, very few policies come anywhere near 50%. At 0.05, the model catches 2,725 of the 6,236 policies with claims, at the cost of 28,708 false alarms.

title: Confusion matrix and threshold metrics
section: Metrics derived from the confusion matrix
text:
Metrics derived from the confusion matrix








Metric
Formula
Question it answers




Accuracy
\(\frac{TP + TN}{N}\)
What share of decisions is correct?


Precision
\(\frac{TP}{TP + FP}\)
Of the flagged policies, what share had a claim?


Recall, true positive rate (TPR), sensitivity
\(\frac{TP}{TP + FN}\)
Of the policies with a claim, what share did we flag?


Specificity, true negative rate (TNR)
\(\frac{TN}{TN + FP}\)
Of the policies without a claim, what share did we leave alone?


False positive rate (FPR)
\(\frac{FP}{FP + TN} = 1 - \text{TNR}\)
Of the policies without a claim, what share did we flag?


F1 score
\(2 \cdot \frac{\text{precision} \cdot \text{recall}}{\text{precision} + \text{recall}}\)
A single summary of precision and recall (their harmonic mean)


Balanced accuracy
\(\frac{\text{TPR} + \text{TNR}}{2}\)
Accuracy if both classes were equally common



Precision and recall look at the positive class from two sides: precision asks how trustworthy a flag is, recall how complete the flagging is. Raising the threshold usually increases precision and decreases recall.

All three models reach an accuracy of about 96.3%, including the Null model, which never predicts a claim. That number is simply the share of policies without a claim. Under class imbalance:

Accuracy is dominated by the majority class. ‘Always predict 0’ reaches 96.3% without learning anything.
Always compare with the Null model. An accuracy only means something next to the accuracy of predicting the majority class (here 96.3%).
Balanced accuracy and recall expose the problem: 0.5 and 0.0 say this decision rule doesn’t find any claims.

The GBM is not useless, though. The problem is the threshold, not the model.

title: Confusion matrix and threshold metrics
text:
Choosing a threshold


Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))
plot_score_distributions(y, b["GBM"], ax=axes[0], threshold=0.05)
plot_threshold_metrics(y, b["GBM"], ax=axes[1])
fig.tight_layout()








Figure 2: Left: predicted claim probabilities of the GBM for policies without and with a claim. Right: threshold metrics of the GBM as the threshold moves.





The left panel shows why no threshold separates the classes cleanly. Policies with a claim get higher probabilities on average, but the two distributions overlap heavily. The right panel shows the resulting trade-off:

Lowering the threshold flags more policies. Recall rises and precision falls.
Accuracy keeps rising with the threshold, because flagging fewer policies means fewer false alarms among the large majority without claims. Maximizing accuracy pushes towards ‘never flag anything’.

So which threshold is right? That depends on what each kind of error costs, not on the model. If a missed claim costs \(c_{FN}\) and a false alarm costs \(c_{FP}\), and the probabilities are calibrated, the cost-minimizing rule is to flag a policy when
\[
\hat p \ge \frac{c_{FP}}{c_{FP} + c_{FN}}.
\]
For example, if a review costs 50 EUR and catching a claim early saves 950 EUR, the optimal threshold is \(50 / (50 + 950) = 0.05\). Decision curves and calibration, covered in later pages, build on this idea.

title: Confusion matrix and threshold metrics
text:
Takeaways

Threshold metrics evaluate a decision rule, so always report the threshold along with them.
Under class imbalance, accuracy mostly measures the class balance. Compare with the Null model, and prefer recall, precision or balanced accuracy.
The threshold should come from the costs of errors, not from the 0.5 default.
To judge the model independently of any one threshold, look at all thresholds at once: that is the ROC curve.

title: Lift charts and Lorenz curves
text:
Question answered: does the model separate low risks from high risks, and is its prediction right for each risk segment?
The deviance page ended with D² values of about 1.3%: individual claims are mostly chance, so any average over individual errors is small. A pricing model is judged on something else: whether the policies it calls expensive really cost more, as a group, than the ones it calls cheap. Grouping averages away the noise. This page covers the standard tools for that:

title: Lift charts and Lorenz curves
text:
The lift chart
To draw a lift chart (also called a quantile plot):

sort the test policies by their predicted pure premium,
cut them into 10 groups (deciles) holding the same total exposure,
per decile, compare the exposure-weighted average prediction with the average actual pure premium.

The deciles hold equal exposure rather than equal numbers of policies, because pure premium is a rate per policy-year: a decile full of short policies would hold far less information than its policy count suggests.


Code
lift = {m: segment_table(y, {m: p[m]}, w, sort_by=p[m]) for m in models}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.2), sharey=True)
for ax, m in zip(axes, models):
    plot_segments(lift[m], [m], ax=ax, xlabel=f"Decile of {m} prediction (1 = lowest)", title=m)
axes[1].set_ylabel("")
fig.tight_layout()








Figure 1: Lift charts on the test set: average actual and predicted pure premium per decile of each model’s prediction (deciles of equal exposure). Bars are 95% intervals for the actual average.





A good lift chart shows three things:

Monotonicity. Actual cost should rise from decile to decile. Both models get there broadly, with a few dips in the middle.
Spread. The steeper the actual curve, the better the model separates risks. The ratio of the top to the bottom decile is a common summary (the ‘lift’ that gives the chart its name).
Agreement. The predicted line should run through the actual points. A gap shows the predictions are off for that segment even when the overall average is right: calibration, checked by group.



Code
pd.DataFrame({
    m: {
        "actual, decile 1 (EUR)": t.loc[1, "actual"],
        "actual, decile 10 (EUR)": t.loc[10, "actual"],
        "lift: decile 10 ÷ decile 1": t.loc[10, "actual"] / t.loc[1, "actual"],
        "lift: decile 10 ÷ overall": t.loc[10, "actual"] / mean,
        "predicted ÷ actual, decile 10": t.loc[10, m] / t.loc[10, "actual"],
    }
    for m, t in lift.items()
}).round(2)

title: Lift charts and Lorenz curves
text:
The double lift chart
Two lift charts side by side are hard to compare: both look good, and their deciles contain different policies. The double lift chart compares the two models directly, on the policies where they disagree:

put both models on the same overall level (here: rescale each so its average on the test set equals the actual average), so a difference in the overall level doesn’t look like a difference in segmentation;
sort the policies by the ratio GBM ÷ GLM, and cut them into deciles of equal exposure;
per decile, compare the actual average with both models’ averages.

Decile 1 holds the policies the GBM rates much lower than the GLM, decile 10 those it rates much higher. In the middle the models agree.

rebalanced = {m: p[m] * mean / np.average(p[m], weights=w) for m in models}
double = segment_table(y, rebalanced, w, sort_by=rebalanced["GBM"] / rebalanced["GLM"])



Code
xlabel = "Decile of GBM ÷ GLM (1 = GBM much lower)"
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.2))
plot_segments(double, models, ax=axes[0], xlabel=xlabel, legend_loc="upper center")
plot_segments(double, models, ax=axes[1], ratio=True, xlabel=xlabel)
fig.tight_layout()








Figure 2: Double lift chart, GBM against GLM. Left: average actual and predicted pure premium per decile of the ratio GBM ÷ GLM. Right: actual ÷ predicted for each model; 1 means the model’s average is right for that decile.





The left panel answers the question ‘who is right where they disagree?’ In decile 1, the GLM predicts 349 EUR, the GBM 182 EUR, and the actual average is 255 EUR. In decile 10, the GLM predicts 104, the GBM 226, and the actual average is 159. Neither model wins: in both tails the truth lies between them.
The right panel shows the same comparison as actual ÷ predicted. The better model is the one whose curve stays flat at 1. Insurers read this as a loss ratio: if premiums were set by the GLM, actual ÷ GLM is the loss ratio each segment would produce.

Actual ÷ GLM rises from 0.73 to 1.53. The GBM finds policies the GLM overprices (left) and underprices (right).
Actual ÷ GBM falls from 1.40 to 0.71. The GLM finds mispricing in the GBM just as well.

Each model knows something the other doesn’t, and each overreacts where it disagrees with the other. A curve that crosses 1 in the opposite direction would mean the model is worse than useless where the two differ: its deviations from the other model point the wrong way.

What the double lift chart suggests: blend
When both models are partly right, a combination usually beats either. A simple blend is the geometric mean of the two predictions (an average on the log scale, which suits multiplicative pricing models):

blend = np.sqrt(rebalanced["GLM"] * rebalanced["GBM"])
blend *= mean / np.average(blend, weights=w)

title: Lift charts and Lorenz curves
section: The Lorenz curve and the Gini index
text:
The Lorenz curve and the Gini index
The lift chart shows separation decile by decile. The Lorenz curve shows it as one continuous curve:

sort the policies from the lowest to the highest prediction,
walk along the sorted list and plot the share of total exposure covered so far (x-axis) against the share of total claim cost it contains (y-axis).

A model that can’t separate risks (the Null model) gives the diagonal: the first 30% of exposure carries 30% of the claim cost. A model that separates well puts little claim cost into its low-risk policies, so its curve sags below the diagonal. The oracle sorts by the actual outcome, the best ranking possible.


Code
ax = plot_lorenz(y, {m: p[m] for m in models}, w)
ax.figure.set_size_inches(5.5, 5.5)








Figure 4: Lorenz curves on the test set, policies sorted from lowest to highest prediction. The dashed curve sorts by the actual outcome.





The GBM’s lowest-risk half of the exposure carries only 32% of the claim cost. The Gini index condenses the curve into one number: twice the area between the diagonal and the curve,
\[
\text{Gini} = 1 - 2 \int_0^1 L(x)\,dx,
\]
where \(L(x)\) is the share of claim cost in the lowest-predicted share \(x\) of the exposure. It is 0 for the Null model and grows the better the model ranks the policies. The two models score 0.293 (GLM) and 0.294 (GBM), a relative difference of 0.6%. On D² the GBM was 6% ahead, and its top-to-bottom lift was much larger. The Gini weighs the whole ranking, while the lift ratio looks only at the two extreme deciles, each resting on a few hundred claims. A single decile ratio is a much noisier summary than the Gini.
The oracle’s Gini of 0.984 is not a realistic target: 95% of the exposure had no claim at all, and only hindsight can put those policies first. Some authors report a normalized Gini (Gini ÷ oracle Gini), but the oracle mostly reflects how many policies happened to have no claims, so it adds little here.






NoteRelation to the classification Gini



The ROC page defined Gini = 2·AUC − 1 for a binary target. For a 0/1 outcome with equal weights, the Lorenz Gini equals \((1 - \pi)(2 \cdot \text{AUC} - 1)\), where \(\pi\) is the share of positives (the tests in tests/ check this). The factor \(1 - \pi\) is the oracle’s Gini: dividing by it gives the normalized Gini, which equals 2·AUC − 1. Both measure how well the model ranks. The Lorenz version extends the idea to outcomes that aren’t 0/1, such as claim cost, and to weighted observations.



What the Gini can’t see
The Gini depends only on the ranking. Any transformation that keeps the order of the predictions leaves it unchanged, however wrong the predictions become:

squared = p["GBM"] ** 2 * np.average(p["GBM"], weights=w) / np.average(p["GBM"] ** 2, weights=w)
variants = {"GBM": p["GBM"], "2 × GBM": 2 * p["GBM"], "GBM squared": squared}
pd.DataFrame({
    name: {
        "Gini": gini_index(y, s, w),
        "D²": deviance_metrics(y, s, p["Null"], w, TWEEDIE_POWER)["D²"],
        "bias (EUR)": regression_metrics(y, s, w)["bias"],
    }
    for name, s in variants.items()
}).round(4)

Doubling every prediction, or squaring them, keeps the Gini exactly the same. D² drops below 0 (worse than predicting the average for everyone), and a lift chart would show the gap at once. So:

Never use the Gini alone. Pair it with a lift chart or a calibration check, and with the deviance.
Don’t compare Ginis across portfolios or years. Like AUC, the Gini depends on how heterogeneous the population is: a portfolio with more varied risks gives a higher Gini for an equally good model.
Small differences are noise. The GLM and GBM differ by 0.002, far less than the test-set variability of a Gini on data this noisy. Testing such differences is the subject of the model-comparison page.

title: Lift charts and Lorenz curves
text:
Takeaways

With noisy outcomes, judge a pricing model on groups: deciles of equal exposure average away the noise that dominates individual-level metrics.
A lift chart should rise monotonically, be steep, and have predictions that run through the actual points. Here the GLM overpredicts its top decile by 23%.
A double lift chart compares two models where they disagree. Here each model finds mispricing in the other, and a simple blend beats both.
The Gini index summarizes the Lorenz curve: 0.293 (GLM) against 0.294 (GBM). It measures ranking only, so a badly miscalibrated model can have the same Gini as a good one.

title: Comparing models
text:
Question answered: is one model really better than another, or did the test set happen to favour it?
Every metric on the earlier pages was computed on one test set of 169,504 policies. A different sample of policies would have given slightly different values, so each metric is an estimate with sampling uncertainty. When two models are close, the question is whether their gap is larger than that uncertainty. This page covers three ways to answer it:
It ends by settling a question left open on the lift chart page: is the GLM–GBM blend’s improvement real?

title: Comparing models
section: Compare the difference, not two intervals
text:
Compare the difference, not two intervals
Both models are scored on the same policies. That matters: a test set that happens to contain many easy-to-rank policies flatters both models at once. Most of the sampling noise is shared, and it cancels in the difference.
The tempting shortcut, computing an interval for each model and checking whether they overlap, ignores this. It treats the two estimates as independent and overstates the uncertainty of the difference, often by a large factor. The right approach measures the uncertainty of the difference itself, on paired data. All three methods below do that.

title: Comparing models
text:
The paired bootstrap
The bootstrap estimates sampling uncertainty by imitating the sampling:

draw a resample of the test set: as many policies as it has, drawn at random with replacement (some appear twice, others not at all);
score both models on the same resample and record their difference;
repeat many times (here 1,000).

The spread of the recorded differences shows how much the difference would vary from one test set to another. Its 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles give a 95% percentile interval.
Here is the AUC of the two HasClaim models from the ROC page:

boot = paired_bootstrap(auc_rank, y, {m: b[m] for m in ("GLM", "GBM")}, n_boot=N_BOOT)



Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.4))
plot_paired_bootstrap(boot, "GBM", "GLM", axes)
fig.tight_layout()








Figure 1: Paired bootstrap of the AUC on the test set. Left: GBM against GLM AUC, one point per resample. Right: distribution of the difference GBM − GLM, with its 95% percentile interval shaded.





The left panel shows why pairing matters. From one resample to the next, the AUCs move together (correlation 0.88): a resample that is easy for the GLM is easy for the GBM too. Each AUC on its own has a standard error of about 0.0033, but their difference only 0.0016. Treating the models as independent would give 0.0047, overstating the uncertainty 2.9 times.

pd.DataFrame({
    **{m: {"AUC": auc[m], "std. error": se[m], "lower": boot[m].quantile(0.025), "upper": boot[m].quantile(0.975)}

    "GBM − GLM": boot_auc.rename({"difference": "AUC"}).drop("p-value"),

NoteWhy the bootstrap works, and when it doesn’t



The bootstrap treats the test set as a stand-in for the population and resamples from it. It works for any metric you can compute, however complicated (AUC, Gini, a lift ratio, the precision in the top 5%), which makes it the default tool. It needs:

Independent observations. Resampling single policies assumes each is a separate draw. With grouped data (several policies per customer) or time series, resample whole groups or blocks instead.
Enough resamples. 1,000 is plenty for a 95% interval. Small p-values need more: with B resamples a p-value can’t go much below 2/B.
Time. Every resample recomputes the metric for every model.

title: Comparing models
text:
DeLong’s test for AUC
For AUC there is a formula that gives the same answer without resampling. DeLong, DeLong and Clarke-Pearson (1988) start from the reading of AUC on the ROC page: the share of (claim, no-claim) pairs that the model orders correctly. That share is an average over pairs, so it splits into a contribution per policy, its placement value:

for a policy with a claim: the share of no-claim policies it outscores;
for a policy without a claim: the share of claim policies that outscore it

(ties count ½). Both sets of placement values average to the AUC, and their variances give the variance of the AUC. For two models, the same computation on the per-policy differences of their placement values gives the variance of the AUC difference, with the pairing built in:
\[
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\text{AUC}}_A - \widehat{\text{AUC}}_B)
= \frac{\operatorname{Var}(V^A_{1} - V^B_{1})}{n_1}
+ \frac{\operatorname{Var}(V^A_{0} - V^B_{0})}{n_0},
\]
where \(V_1\) are the placement values of the \(n_1\) claim policies and \(V_0\) those of the \(n_0\) no-claim policies. The test statistic is the difference divided by its standard error, compared with the normal distribution.

delong = delong_test(y, b["GBM"], b["GLM"])
comparison_table({"DeLong": delong, "Paired bootstrap": boot_auc})

The two methods agree closely: DeLong’s standard error is 0.00165, the bootstrap’s 0.00163. DeLong’s p-value can go far below anything 1,000 resamples could show, and it takes a fraction of a second. For AUC alone, DeLong is the standard choice. For other metrics, use the bootstrap.

title: Comparing models
text:
The Diebold–Mariano test for losses
Log loss, the Brier score, squared error and deviance are all averages of a loss per observation. Comparing two models on such a metric is comparing two averages over the same observations. Diebold and Mariano (1995) test this through the loss differential of each observation,
\[
d_i = L(y_i, \hat y^A_i) - L(y_i, \hat y^B_i),
\]
whose average is the difference in the metric. If the models are equally good, the \(d_i\) average to 0 apart from noise. The test divides \(\bar d\) by its standard error, \(\text{sd}(d) / \sqrt n\), and compares the result with the normal distribution. With weights (such as exposure) both the average and its standard error are weighted.
For independent observations this is simply a paired test on the losses. The name comes from forecasting, where the observations form a time series: there the standard error must allow for autocorrelation between consecutive \(d_i\) (a Newey–West standard error), which is the original test’s real contribution.

p_glm, p_gbm = b["GLM"].to_numpy(), b["GBM"].to_numpy()
log_loss_per_policy = lambda p: -(y * np.log(p) + (1 - y) * np.log(1 - p))
comparison_table({
    "log loss": diebold_mariano(log_loss_per_policy(p_glm), log_loss_per_policy(p_gbm)),
    "Brier score": diebold_mariano((p_glm - y) ** 2, (p_gbm - y) ** 2),
})

The GBM’s log loss is 2.2% lower than the GLM’s, a small relative gain but measured very precisely: on a large test set even small differences in an average loss are easy to detect. The probabilities agree with the ranking from the AUC tests. The GBM is better on both.
Two things the Diebold–Mariano test can’t do:

AUC and Gini are not averages of per-observation losses. They depend on pairs or on the ranking of the whole test set, so they have no loss differential. Use DeLong or the bootstrap.
It compares scores, not truth. A significant difference in log loss says one model’s probabilities are closer to the outcomes on average. It says nothing about where: for that, look at calibration plots and double lift charts.

title: Comparing models
text:
Is the blend’s improvement real?
The lift chart page found that the GLM and the GBM for pure premium each detect mispricing in the other, and that their geometric mean beats both. But all three Gini indices lay within about 0.015 of each other, on a target where a few large claims dominate everything. Time to test.
One detail first. On the lift chart page, the blend was rescaled so that its average on the test set matched the actual average. That uses the test outcomes, which would flatter the blend’s deviance. Here the scale factor comes from the training set, so nothing about the blend is fitted on the test data. (The Gini doesn’t depend on the scale, so it is unchanged.)

pp = pure_premium_predictions()
yp, w = pp["y"].to_numpy(), pp["w"].to_numpy()

train, fitted = train_test().train, load_models()["pure_premium"]
glm_train, gbm_train = (fitted[m].predict(train[FEATURES]) for m in ("GLM", "GBM"))
scale = np.average(train["PurePremium"], weights=train["Exposure"]) / np.average(
    np.sqrt(glm_train * gbm_train), weights=train["Exposure"]
)
scores = {m: pp[m].to_numpy() for m in ("GLM", "GBM")}
scores["Blend"] = scale * np.sqrt(scores["GLM"] * scores["GBM"])

We compare all three pairs on two metrics:

the Gini index, a ranking metric with no per-policy loss: paired bootstrap, resampling policies together with their exposure;
D², the share of the Null model’s Tweedie deviance explained: the Diebold–Mariano test on the per-policy deviance, weighted by exposure. Since all models share the same Null deviance, a difference in D² is a difference in mean deviance divided by the Null deviance.


pairs = [("GBM", "GLM"), ("Blend", "GLM"), ("Blend", "GBM")]
gini = {m: gini_index(yp, s, w) for m, s in scores.items()}
gini_boot = paired_bootstrap(gini_index, yp, scores, w, n_boot=N_BOOT)
gini_tests = {f"{a} − {c}": bootstrap_summary(gini[a] - gini[c], gini_boot[a] - gini_boot[c]) for a, c in pairs}

deviance = {m: tweedie_deviance(yp, s, TWEEDIE_POWER) for m, s in scores.items()}
null_deviance = np.average(tweedie_deviance(yp, pp["Null"], TWEEDIE_POWER), weights=w)
d2_tests = {}
for a, c in pairs:
    dm = diebold_mariano(deviance[c], deviance[a], w)  # positive: model a has lower deviance
    scaled = ["difference", "std. error", "lower", "upper"]
    d2_tests[f"{a} − {c}"] = pd.concat([dm[scaled] / null_deviance, dm[["p-value"]]])



Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.2), sharey=True)
plot_intervals(pd.DataFrame(gini_tests).T, ax=axes[0], xlabel="Difference in Gini index", title="Gini (ranking)")
plot_intervals(pd.DataFrame(d2_tests).T, ax=axes[1], xlabel="Difference in D²", title="D² (deviance)")
fig.tight_layout()

Three conclusions, from clear to uncertain:

GBM against GLM: no detectable difference. The Gini difference is +0.002 with an interval from -0.025 to 0.028, and the D² difference is just as inconclusive (p = 0.619). The GBM’s clearly better AUC for HasClaim does not carry over to pure premium, where claim sizes add a large amount of noise.
Blend against GLM: likely better. Both intervals exclude 0 (p = 0.018 for the Gini, 0.012 for D²). That is good evidence, though not overwhelming (see the next section).
Blend against GBM: suggestive, not established. Both intervals include 0: the Gini gain of 0.013 has p = 0.084, the D² gain p = 0.093.

The pairing is again what makes any of this detectable. Each Gini on its own has a bootstrap standard error of about 0.028, so the per-model intervals overlap almost completely, yet the blend’s difference from the GLM has a standard error of only 0.006. The blend is built from the GLM and the GBM, so its ranking is close to both, and most of the noise cancels.
Why are the intervals so wide? The test set has only 6,236 policies with a claim, and claim costs range over several orders of magnitude. For the deviance comparison of blend and GBM, the 170 policies that contribute most (the top 0.1%) account for 96% of the variance of the loss differential. A handful of large claims decide the result, so the test is far less precise than the size of the test set suggests.

Before declaring a winner
Six tests, not one. This section ran three comparisons on two metrics. With six chances, one p-value below 0.05 is less convincing than it looks. The simplest correction (Bonferroni) asks for p below 0.05 / 6 ≈ 0.008 for each test, and neither blend result passes it. The blend’s gain over the GLM is still the most credible finding: both metrics point the same way, and the double lift chart explained why blending should help before we tested it. But it should be confirmed on fresh data before anyone relies on it.
The blend was suggested by the test set. We tried it because the double lift chart, drawn on these same test policies, pointed to it. A 50/50 blend has no tuned parameter and its scale comes from the training data, so the risk of having fitted the test set is small. Had we tuned the blend’s weight on the test set, its test-set score would be optimistic and the tests above invalid. The clean procedure: choose the blend on a validation set, or on cross-validation folds of the training data, and test once on held-out data.
Statistical is not practical significance. A p-value says whether a difference is distinguishable from noise, not whether it matters. The GBM’s 2.2% lower log loss is overwhelmingly significant but may not justify replacing a GLM that regulators and underwriters understand. Report the interval for the difference, and judge whether its whole range would change a decision.






NoteWhat these tests leave out: the training sample



All three methods resample the test set. They answer: ‘are these two fitted models different on the population the test set comes from?’ That is the right question when deciding which fitted model to deploy. They ignore that training on a different sample would have produced different models. To ask whether one modelling approach beats another (GBMs against GLMs in general, on this kind of data), repeat the fitting across cross-validation folds or repeated splits, and use a test that accounts for the overlap between training sets, such as the corrected resampled t-test of Nadeau and Bengio (2003).

title: Comparing models
text:
Takeaways

A metric computed on a test set is an estimate. Before preferring one model, check whether the gap is larger than its sampling uncertainty.
Pair the comparison. Both models are scored on the same observations, so test the difference directly. Overlapping per-model intervals say little: here the paired standard error was 2.9 times smaller than the unpaired one for AUC.
The paired bootstrap works for any metric. DeLong’s test gives the same answer for AUC instantly. The Diebold–Mariano test handles any average loss, such as log loss or deviance.
For HasClaim, the GBM beats the GLM beyond doubt. For pure premium, GBM and GLM are indistinguishable. The blend is likely better than the GLM (p = 0.018 and 0.012, not robust to a correction for multiple tests), and its edge over the GBM is suggestive but not established on this test set.
Watch for multiple comparisons, for choices made on the test set, and for the difference between statistical and practical significance.

title: Measuring model performance
text: This project documents how to measure the performance of predictive models, working through every method on real models fitted to real data. Each page answers one question about a model, shows the method on our examples, and explains when it misleads.

title: Measuring model performance
text:
How the pages are organized
Metrics are grouped by the question they answer rather than listed by name:

Classification at a threshold: is the yes/no decision right? (confusion matrix)
Discrimination: does the model rank cases correctly? (ROC and AUC, precision–recall)
Calibration: do predicted probabilities match observed frequencies? (calibration and scoring rules)
Error size: how far off are the predictions? (error metrics, deviance)
Ranking and segmentation: does the model separate low risks from high risks? (lift charts and Lorenz curves)
Model comparison: is one model really better, or is the gap noise? (comparing models)
Drift: coming next.

text:
The four basic metrics
With errors \(e_i = \hat y_i - y_i\) over \(n\) test cases:









Metric
Formula
Unit
Question it answers




Bias (mean error)
\(\frac{1}{n}\sum e_i\)
target
Is the model systematically too high or too low?


MAE (mean absolute error)
\(\frac{1}{n}\sum \lvert e_i \rvert\)
target
How large is a typical error?


RMSE (root mean squared error)
\(\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum e_i^2}\)
target
How large are errors, with big ones weighted more?


R² (coefficient of determination)
\(1 - \frac{\sum e_i^2}{\sum (y_i - \bar y)^2}\)
none
What share of the variance does the model explain?



With weights \(w_i\) (as for pure premium, weighted by exposure), each sum becomes a weighted sum and \(n\) becomes \(\sum w_i\).

Reading the table:

title: Error metrics: bias, MAE, RMSE and R²
text:
What MAE and RMSE reward
MAE and RMSE don’t just weigh errors differently, they reward different predictions:

Squared error is minimized by the mean. A model trained or selected on RMSE learns the conditional mean of the target.
Absolute error is minimized by the median. A model selected on MAE learns the conditional median.

For a symmetric target the two coincide. For a skewed target, such as house prices, claim costs or incomes, they don’t. Scoring every constant prediction shows this:


Code
c = np.linspace(0.5, 4.0, 200)
mae = [np.mean(np.abs(y - v)) for v in c]
rmse = [np.sqrt(np.mean((y - v) ** 2)) for v in c]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.8))
for values, name, color in [(mae, "MAE", METRIC_COLORS[0]), (rmse, "RMSE", METRIC_COLORS[1])]:
    ax.plot(c, values, color=color, label=name)
    ax.annotate(name, (c[-1], values[-1]), xytext=(4, 0), textcoords="offset points",
                va="center", fontsize=9, color=INK_SECONDARY)
for stat, value, side in [("median", y.median(), -1), ("mean", y.mean(), 1)]:
    ax.axvline(value, color=INK_SECONDARY, linewidth=1)
    ax.annotate(f"{stat} {value:.2f}", (value, 1), xycoords=("data", "axes fraction"),
                xytext=(4 * side, -4), textcoords="offset points", va="top",
                ha="left" if side > 0 else "right", fontsize=9, color=INK_SECONDARY)
ax.set(xlabel="Constant prediction (100k USD)", ylabel="Error (100k USD)")
ax.legend(loc="lower right")








Figure 1: MAE and RMSE of predicting the same constant value for every district.





The MAE curve bottoms out at the median, the RMSE curve at the mean. So choosing a metric is choosing what the model should predict. For pricing, where the average cost must be covered, the mean is the right target and squared-error-type metrics are the right family. MAE answers a different question.






WarningMAPE and other relative errors



The mean absolute percentage error, \(\frac{1}{n}\sum \lvert e_i / y_i \rvert\), is popular because it is unit-free. It is undefined when \(y_i = 0\), explodes when \(y_i\) is small, and penalizes over-prediction more than under-prediction, which pushes models to predict too low. Use it only for targets well away from zero, and never for pure premium.

title: Error metrics: bias, MAE, RMSE and R²
text:
Looking at the errors
A single number hides where a model errs. Two plots do most of the work:

actual vs predicted: points should scatter evenly around the diagonal,
residuals vs predicted: residuals should scatter evenly around zero, with no trend, no fan shape and no visible structure.



Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(9, 8.5))
for col, m in enumerate(("GLM", "GBM")):
    plot_actual_vs_predicted(y, h[m], ax=axes[0, col], title=m)
    plot_residuals(y, h[m], ax=axes[1, col])
fig.tight_layout()








Figure 2: Actual vs predicted (top; the diagonal marks perfect prediction) and residuals vs predicted (bottom) for the GLM and the GBM. Color shows the number of districts per hexagon, on a log scale.





Three things stand out, none of which the metrics table shows:

A horizontal line at 5.0 (a diagonal stripe in the residual plots). 4.6% of districts have a value of exactly 5.0, because values were capped when the data was collected. The true values are higher, so the errors there are partly an artifact of the data, not of the model.
The GLM’s residuals trend downward. It under-predicts cheap districts and over-predicts expensive ones: the relationship isn’t linear, and a linear model can’t bend to follow it. It also predicts outside the possible range for 1.3% of districts (above the cap or below zero).
The GBM’s residuals are tighter and centered on zero across the whole range, consistent with its lower RMSE, but they widen for expensive districts. The errors are larger where values are larger, which is common for prices and amounts.

Where these metrics break: pure premium
Now apply the same metrics to pure premium, weighted by exposure. We add one more ‘model’: predicting 0 for every policy.

preds = {m: p[m] for m in ("Null", "GLM", "GBM")} | {"Always 0": np.zeros(len(p))}

The results are strange:

‘Always 0’ has the best MAE (146 against 271 for the GBM). Most policies have no claim, so the median pure premium is 0, and MAE rewards the median. A pricing model that charges nothing would win on MAE.
RMSE is nearly identical for all models (about 4,044). It’s dominated by a few huge claims spread over short exposures, which no model can predict.
R² is about 0.0005 for both models: practically zero, even though, as the next pages show, both models clearly separate low and high risks.

The problem isn’t the models. These metrics assume errors of similar size everywhere, and for insurance targets that assumption fails badly: most outcomes are exactly zero, the rest vary enormously, and the variance grows with the expected value. Such targets need a loss that matches their distribution: the deviance.

title: Error metrics: bias, MAE, RMSE and R²
text:
Takeaways

Bias checks systematic over- or under-prediction; MAE and RMSE give the typical error size in the target’s unit; R² compares with the Null model.
Choosing a metric chooses what the model should predict: RMSE rewards the mean, MAE the median.
Plot the residuals. Capped data, non-linear effects and growing error variance stay invisible in summary metrics.
For zero-heavy, skewed targets such as pure premium, MAE, RMSE and R² are misleading. Use deviance and ranking-based measures instead.

title: Deviance and D²
text:
Question answered: how well do the predictions fit, measured in a way that respects the target’s distribution?
The previous page ended with MAE, RMSE and R² failing on pure premium. This page introduces the metric the models were actually trained on: the deviance.

title: Deviance and D²
text:
Why squared error doesn’t fit
Squared error treats an error of 100 EUR the same everywhere. That makes sense when every observation is equally noisy. For insurance targets, the noise grows with the expected value: a risk expected to cost 1,000 EUR a year varies far more than one expected to cost 50 EUR. In the Tweedie family of distributions, used for such targets, this is explicit:
\[
\operatorname{Var}(Y) = \phi \, \mu^{p},
\]
where \(\mu\) is the expected value, \(\phi\) a dispersion parameter, and the power \(p\) describes how fast the variance grows with the mean.








Power \(p\)
Distribution
Typical target




0
Normal
errors of constant size (house prices, roughly)


1
Poisson

1 < p < 2
compound Poisson–Gamma
pure premium: exactly 0 often, otherwise positive amounts


2
Gamma

Our pure premium GLM uses \(p = 1\.9\).

title: Deviance and D²
text:
The deviance
The unit deviance \(d(y, \mu)\) measures how far the prediction \(\mu\) is from the outcome \(y\), on the scale the distribution implies. For the Tweedie family with \(1 < p < 2\):
\[
d(y, \mu) = 2 \left( \frac{y^{2-p}}{(1-p)(2-p)} - \frac{y\,\mu^{1-p}}{1-p} + \frac{\mu^{2-p}}{2-p} \right).
\]
It’s twice the log-likelihood gap between a perfect prediction and \(\mu\), so minimizing the mean deviance is maximum likelihood: the same criterion the GLM is fitted with. At \(p = 0\) it reduces to squared error, so squared error is just the deviance for a normal distribution.
Two properties make it suitable for pure premium:

Errors are judged relative to the expected level. Missing by 100 EUR on a risk expected to cost 50 EUR counts more than missing by 100 EUR on a risk expected to cost 2,000 EUR.
Predictions must be positive. Predicting \(\mu = 0\) for a risk that can have claims gives an infinite deviance. ‘Always 0’, which won on MAE, is ruled out.



Code
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
# Compound Poisson-Gamma outcomes with mean 200: claims with probability ~5%, average size ~4,000
n_claims = rng.poisson(0.05, 200_000)
outcomes = np.array([rng.gamma(2.0, 2000.0, k).sum() for k in n_claims])
mu = np.linspace(20, 800, 150)
tweedie = np.array([tweedie_deviance(outcomes, m, TWEEDIE_POWER).mean() for m in mu])
squared = np.array([np.mean((outcomes - m) ** 2) for m in mu])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.8))
for curve, name, color in [(squared, "squared error", METRIC_COLORS[0]),
                           (tweedie, f"Tweedie deviance (p = {TWEEDIE_POWER})", METRIC_COLORS[1])]:
    excess = curve - curve.min()
    scale = excess[np.argmin(np.abs(mu - 100))]
    ax.plot(mu, excess / scale, color=color, label=name)
ax.axvline(outcomes.mean(), color=INK_SECONDARY, linewidth=1)
ax.annotate(f"true mean {outcomes.mean():.0f}", (outcomes.mean(), 1), xycoords=("data", "axes fraction"),
            xytext=(4, -4), textcoords="offset points", va="top", fontsize=9, color=INK_SECONDARY)
ax.set(xlabel="Prediction μ (EUR)", ylabel="Extra loss vs best prediction\n(relative)", ylim=(0, 3))
ax.legend(loc="upper right", bbox_to_anchor=(1, 0.88))








Figure 1: Penalty for predicting μ when the expected value is 200 EUR: squared error (scaled to match at μ = 100) against Tweedie deviance with p = 1.9, averaged over a simulated outcome distribution with that mean.





Both losses are minimized at the true mean, so both reward predicting the mean. They differ in how they punish a miss: squared error is symmetric, so predicting 0 costs as much as predicting double the mean. The deviance punishes under-prediction much harder, because a low \(\mu\) claims that large outcomes are nearly impossible.

title: Deviance and D²
section: D²: the deviance version of R²
text:
D²: the deviance version of R²
Like R², the fraction of deviance explained compares a model with the Null model:
\[
D^2 = 1 - \frac{\sum_i w_i\, d(y_i, \hat\mu_i)}{\sum_i w_i\, d(y_i, \bar y)}.
\]
With \(p = 0\) it equals R². Like R², it is 0 for the Null model, can be negative for a model worse than the mean, and can’t be compared across datasets.

pd.DataFrame({
    m: pd.concat([deviance_metrics(y, p[m], p["Null"], w, TWEEDIE_POWER),
                  regression_metrics(y, p[m], w)[["bias", "R²"]]])
    for m in ("Null", "GLM", "GBM")
}).round(4)

Compared with R², the deviance gives a clearer picture:

Both models explain about 1.3% of the deviance, roughly 26 times their R² (0.05% for the GBM): R² was drowned out by a few huge claims.
The GBM is slightly ahead of the GLM (1.34% against 1.27%). Whether a difference this small is real, and not test-set noise, is a question for the model-comparison page.


Is a D² this small good?
Yes: values like this are normal for individual insurance outcomes. Whether a given policy has a claim this year is mostly chance, and no model can predict chance. A pricing model’s job isn’t to predict which policy will claim but to separate low risks from high risks. That ability shows up clearly in ranking and segmentation tools (Lorenz curves, Gini, lift and double lift charts), which barely react to the noise that dominates individual-level metrics. They are covered on the next page.

Choosing the power
The deviance depends on \(p\), and models can rank differently under different powers. A quick sensitivity check:


Code

    f"p = {pw}": {m: deviance_metrics(y, p[m], p["Null"], w, pw)["D²"] for m in ("GLM", "GBM")}
    for pw in (1.2, 1.5, 1.9)
}).round(4)

Here the GBM stays ahead under every power, but the level of D² changes a lot with \(p\). A D² is only meaningful together with the power it was computed with. Pick \(p\) to match the target, ideally the power used to train the model or one estimated from the data, and keep it fixed when comparing models. If the ranking of models flips between plausible powers, neither model is clearly better.






NoteA note on weights



Pure premium is a rate per policy-year, so a policy observed for a week gives a very noisy rate. Weighting each policy’s deviance by its exposure gives a one-week policy 1/52 of the weight of a full-year policy, consistent with how the models were fitted. Unweighted metrics would be dominated by short policies with extreme rates.

title: Deviance and D²
text:
Takeaways

The deviance is the error measure that matches the target’s distribution, and it’s what GLMs and GBMs actually minimize.
For insurance targets use Tweedie (pure premium), Poisson (frequency) or Gamma (severity) deviance, with exposure or claim-count weights.
D² is the fraction of the Null model’s deviance explained. Small values are normal when outcomes are mostly chance.
When individual outcomes are this noisy, ranking and segmentation measures show a model’s value better than any average error.

title: Precision–recall curves
text: Question answered: of the cases the model flags, how many are real positives, and how many of the real positives does it find?

title: Precision–recall curves
text:
Why look beyond ROC
The ROC curve measures false alarms relative to all negatives: the false positive rate is FP / (FP + TN). With 96.3% of policies without a claim, that denominator is huge, and a small false positive rate can hide a large number of false alarms:
At a threshold of 0.1, the GBM has a false positive rate of only 3.3%: a point far to the left on the ROC curve. But that is 5,412 false alarms against 1,180 correctly flagged claims, so only 18% of the flagged policies actually have a claim.
Precision relates false alarms to true hits instead of to all negatives, so it shows directly what happens among the flagged cases. That makes it the natural metric when positives are rare and attention goes to the cases the model flags: fraud checks, claim reviews, medical screening, marketing campaigns.

title: Precision–recall curves
text:
The precision–recall curve
The PR curve uses the same threshold sweep as the ROC curve, but plots

recall (true positive rate: the share of all claims we flag) on the x-axis, against
precision (the share of flagged policies with a claim) on the y-axis.

Starting from a very high threshold, only the highest-risk policies are flagged: recall is small and, for a good model, precision is high. Lowering the threshold raises recall and, usually, lowers precision, until everything is flagged: recall 1 and precision equal to the overall claim rate.


Code
ax = plot_pr(y, {m: b[m] for m in models}, ylim=0.5)








Figure 1: Precision–recall curves on the test set. Thin gray curves connect points with the same F1 score.





Three things differ from a ROC plot:

The baseline is the claim rate, not a diagonal. Flagging at random gives a precision equal to the claim rate (3.7%) at every recall.
The curve isn’t monotone. Precision can go up or down when the threshold drops, so the curve is jagged, especially on the left where few policies are flagged and each one changes precision noticeably.
The left part matters most. It shows the highest-risk policies, which is where a review or intervention would start. Here the GBM clearly beats the GLM, even though their ROC curves were close.

The gray curves connect points of equal F1 score, the harmonic mean of precision and recall. The best F1 the GBM reaches is 0.185 (at threshold 0.10), against 0.153 for the GLM. Low values like these are typical for rare events. F1 is only a convenient summary: it weights precision and recall equally, which rarely matches the actual costs of misses and false alarms.

title: Precision–recall curves
text:
Average precision
Average precision (AP) condenses the PR curve into one number: the precision at each threshold, weighted by how much recall that threshold adds,
\[
\text{AP} = \sum_k (R_k - R_{k-1})\, P_k,
\]
where \(R_k\) and \(P_k\) are recall and precision after lowering the threshold past the \(k\)-th distinct score. The Null model’s AP equals the claim rate.
Using the same ten toy policies as on the ROC page:

toy_y = np.array([1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0])
toy_p = np.array([0.9, 0.8, 0.7, 0.6, 0.55, 0.5, 0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1])
toy = pr_points(toy_y, toy_p)
toy["AP contribution"] = np.diff(np.r_[0, toy["recall"]]) * toy["precision"]

WarningDon’t use the trapezoidal area



Computing the area under the PR curve with the trapezoidal rule (as for ROC) connects the points with straight lines. Between two PR points, precision does not change linearly, so the result is off, in either direction, and it also depends on which starting point is assumed at recall 0. On the toy example it gives 0.811 instead of 0.830. With many distinct scores the gap shrinks, but AP is the well-defined summary: average_precision_score in scikit-learn, whereas sklearn.metrics.auc on a PR curve is the trapezoidal version.

Precision and lift in the top k%

title: Precision–recall curves
section: Precision depends on the claim rate
text:
Precision depends on the claim rate
Precision has a property that matters a lot in practice: unlike the ROC curve, it depends on the base rate. At any threshold,
\[
\text{precision} = \frac{\pi \cdot \text{TPR}}{\pi \cdot \text{TPR} + (1 - \pi) \cdot \text{FPR}},
\]
where \(\pi\) is the share of positives. TPR and FPR are properties of the model alone. Precision mixes them with \(\pi\). To see the effect, we keep all policies with a claim and randomly drop policies without a claim until the claim rate reaches 10%, 20% and 50%. The model and its ranking don’t change.

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
pos, neg = np.flatnonzero(y == 1), np.flatnonzero(y == 0)
samples = {}
for target in (rate, 0.10, 0.20, 0.50):
    n_neg = min(len(neg), int(len(pos) * (1 - target) / target))
    idx = np.r_[pos, rng.choice(neg, n_neg, replace=False)]
    samples[f"{target:.1%}"] = (y.to_numpy()[idx], b["GBM"].to_numpy()[idx])



Code
ramp = ["#86b6ef", "#3987e5", "#1c5cab", "#0d366b"]  # light to dark: rising claim rate
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.6))
axes[0].plot([0, 1], [0, 1], color=MUTED, linewidth=1)
for (label, (ys, ps)), color in zip(samples.items(), ramp):
    roc, pr = roc_points(ys, ps), pr_points(ys, ps)
    axes[0].plot(roc["fpr"], roc["tpr"], color=color, label=f"claim rate {label} (AUC {auc_rank(ys, ps):.3f})")
    axes[1].plot(np.r_[0, pr["recall"]], np.r_[pr["precision"].iloc[0], pr["precision"]],
                 drawstyle="steps-pre", color=color, label=f"claim rate {label} (AP {average_precision(ys, ps):.3f})")
axes[0].set(xlabel="False positive rate", ylabel="True positive rate", xlim=(0, 1), ylim=(0, 1.01), aspect="equal")
axes[1].set(xlabel="Recall", ylabel="Precision", xlim=(0, 1), ylim=(0, 1.01))
axes[0].legend(loc="lower right")
axes[1].legend(loc="upper right")
fig.tight_layout()








Figure 2: The same GBM evaluated at different claim rates (by subsampling policies without a claim). Left: ROC curves. Right: precision–recall curves.





The ROC curves lie on top of each other: AUC doesn’t change. The PR curves rise with the claim rate, and AP climbs from 0.12 to 0.71. Same model, same ranking, different AP. This has practical consequences:

Don’t compare AP across datasets, segments or time periods with different base rates. A higher AP may only mean more positives. Report the base rate next to every AP, or report AP / base rate.
Balanced test sets inflate precision. Undersampling negatives, common in fraud and medical studies, makes precision look far better than it will be in production.
Precision drifts when the base rate drifts. If the claim rate drops next year, the precision of the same model at the same threshold drops too, even though nothing about the model has changed. This is one reason to monitor the base rate along with model metrics.

title: Precision–recall curves
text:
ROC or PR?
The two curves contain the same information (given the base rate, every ROC point maps to exactly one PR point), but they emphasize different things:

It’s often claimed that AP is ‘the right metric for imbalanced data’. That’s too simple. Imbalance alone doesn’t make AUC wrong. Recent work (McDermott et al., 2024) shows that AP favors improvements at the top of the ranking and can favor models that work best for the subgroups with the highest base rates. Choose by the question: use AUC when the whole ranking matters, AP or precision at k% when only the top of the ranking is acted on, and report the base rate with any precision-based metric.

title: Precision–recall curves
text:
Takeaways

Precision relates false alarms to true hits, which is what matters when positives are rare and only flagged cases are acted on.
The PR curve’s baseline is the base rate. Average precision is its correct summary; don’t use the trapezoidal area.
AP weights the top of the ranking. Here it shows the GBM’s advantage (24%) much more clearly than AUC (3%).
With fixed capacity, report precision and lift at k%.
Precision and AP depend on the base rate. Never compare them across populations with different base rates, and watch them change when the base rate drifts.

title: Calibration and proper scoring rules
text:
Question answered: when the model says 10%, does the event happen about 10% of the time?
The ROC page ended with a warning: AUC only measures ranking. A model can rank perfectly and still predict probabilities that are far off. Whenever the probabilities themselves are used, for a premium, an expected cost, a capital estimate or the cost-based threshold, they must also be calibrated.

title: Calibration and proper scoring rules
text:
What calibration means
A model is calibrated if, among all cases that receive prediction \(\hat p\), the event happens with frequency \(\hat p\):
\[
P(Y = 1 \mid \hat p = p) = p \quad \text{for all } p.
\]
Calibration and discrimination are separate properties:

Always predicting the overall claim rate (the Null model) is perfectly calibrated but has no discrimination.
Dividing every GBM prediction by 10 keeps the discrimination but ruins calibration.

A good model needs both.

title: Calibration and proper scoring rules
text:
Reliability diagrams
A reliability diagram plots the observed rate against the predicted probability. A calibrated model follows the diagonal. Points above the diagonal mean the model predicts too low there, points below mean too high.

The classic version: binning
The usual recipe sorts the cases by prediction, splits them into bins (here 20 bins with equal numbers of policies), and plots each bin’s average prediction against its observed claim rate:


Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 4.5))
for ax, m in zip(axes, ("GLM", "GBM")):
    plot_reliability(y, {m: b[m]}, ax=ax, method="bins", title=m)
fig.tight_layout()








Figure 1: Binned reliability diagrams: 20 bins of equal size, with 95% confidence intervals for the observed rate.





Both models stay close to the diagonal over most of the range. Most policies have a predicted probability below 10%, so the bins are packed there and sparse above. The few high-risk bins carry wide confidence intervals.


The problem with bins
The picture depends on how the bins are chosen, and there’s no right choice. The same GBM with different binnings:


Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 4.2))
for ax, (n, strategy) in zip(axes, [(10, "uniform"), (10, "quantile"), (100, "quantile")]):
    plot_reliability(y, {"GBM": b["GBM"]}, ax=ax, method="bins", n_bins=n, strategy=strategy,
                     max_p=0.35, title=f"{n} {'equal-width' if strategy == 'uniform' else 'equal-count'} bins")
    ax.get_legend().remove()
fig.tight_layout()








Figure 2: The GBM’s reliability diagram under three binning choices.





Equal-width bins put nearly all policies in the first two bins and leave the rest nearly empty. Few equal-count bins hide any detail at the high end. Many bins turn the diagram into noise. Summary statistics built on bins inherit the problem. The expected calibration error (ECE), the share-weighted average gap between bin prediction and bin rate, changes with the binning:

With 100 bins, the GBM’s ECE is 7 times larger than with 5 bins. That’s not because the model got worse: smaller bins simply contain more sampling noise. ECE values are only comparable at the same binning, and even then mostly measure noise when bins are small.


The modern version: CORP
The CORP approach (consistent, optimally binned, reproducible; Dimitriadis, Gneiting and Jordan, 2021) replaces hand-chosen bins with isotonic regression. It finds the best non-decreasing step function mapping predictions to observed outcomes, using the pool-adjacent-violators (PAV) algorithm. In effect, the data chooses the bins: adjacent predictions are merged exactly where their outcomes don’t support a higher rate.

No tuning: no bin count or bin edges to choose, so the result is reproducible.
Consistent: with more data, the curve converges to the true calibration curve.
Uncertainty built in: simulating outcomes from the model’s own probabilities shows how much a perfectly calibrated model’s curve wobbles by chance. The 90% range of these simulations is the consistency band. Where the observed curve leaves the band, the miscalibration is real.

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 4.5))
for ax, m in zip(axes, ("GLM", "GBM")):
    plot_reliability(y, {m: b[m]}, ax=ax, method="corp", band=True, title=m)
fig.tight_layout()








Figure 3: CORP reliability diagrams with 90% consistency bands (200 simulations each).





Both curves follow the diagonal closely where most policies are, below about 6%. Above that, both tend to run above the diagonal, and the GLM’s curve leaves its band several times. Both models under-predict their highest risks, the GLM more clearly. The segment analysis below shows where this comes from. In practice, the CORP diagram should be the default, and binned diagrams kept for audiences used to them.

Calibration intercept and slope
Two numbers summarize the most common patterns of miscalibration. Fit a logistic regression of the outcome on the model’s logit,
\[
\operatorname{logit} P(Y = 1) = a + b \cdot \operatorname{logit}(\hat p),
\]
and read off:

title: Calibration and proper scoring rules
text:
Proper scoring rules
Calibration plots diagnose. To compare models with a single number that rewards both calibration and discrimination, use a proper scoring rule. It’s a score whose expected value is best when the predicted probability equals the true probability, so no forecaster can improve their expected score by reporting anything other than what they believe. The two standard ones, lower is better for both:
\[
\text{Brier score} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i} (\hat p_i - y_i)^2,
\qquad
\text{log loss} = -\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i} \big[ y_i \log \hat p_i + (1 - y_i)\log(1 - \hat p_i) \big].
\]

Brier score: squared error on probabilities. It’s bounded and robust, but small differences are hard to see when events are rare.
Log loss: the negative log-likelihood, and exactly what logistic regression and the GBM were trained on. It punishes confident wrong predictions without limit: predicting 0.1% for a policy that does have a claim costs far more than predicting 10% for one that doesn’t.

Accuracy, F1 and AUC are not proper scoring rules. Accuracy and F1 only see which side of a threshold a prediction falls on, and AUC only sees ranking. A model can improve on them while its probabilities get worse.

The Murphy decomposition
A raw score is hard to interpret on its own. The CORP decomposition splits any proper score exactly into three parts:
\[
\text{score} = \underbrace{\text{MCB}}_{\text{miscalibration}} - \underbrace{\text{DSC}}_{\text{discrimination}} + \underbrace{\text{UNC}}_{\text{uncertainty}}.
\]

UNC: the score of the Null model, i.e. how hard the problem is. It’s the same for every model on the same data.
DSC: how much the score improves when the predictions are optimally recalibrated (isotonic regression), compared with the Null model. It depends only on the ranking, like AUC. Higher is better.
MCB: how much worse the actual predictions score than their recalibrated version: the price paid for miscalibration. Lower is better.

title: Calibration and proper scoring rules
text:
Calibration within segments
Overall calibration can hide miscalibration in subgroups, and subgroups are often what matters, such as tariff cells, customer segments or regions. Insurers check this with the actual-to-expected (A/E) ratio: observed claims divided by predicted claims, per segment. A/E above 1 means the model predicts too low for that segment.


Code
test = train_test().test
segment = pd.cut(test["BonusMalus"], [0, 50, 60, 80, 100, 250],
                 labels=["50 (best)", "51–60", "61–80", "81–100", "> 100 (malus)"])
df = b.assign(segment=segment.to_numpy())
grouped = df.groupby("segment", observed=True)
ae = pd.DataFrame({
    "Policies": grouped.size(),
    "Observed rate": grouped["y"].mean(),
    "A/E GLM": grouped["y"].sum() / grouped["GLM"].sum(),
    "A/E GBM": grouped["y"].sum() / grouped["GBM"].sum(),

TipFixing miscalibration



If ranking is good but probabilities are off, a model can be recalibrated by mapping its predictions through a fitted function:

Platt scaling (logistic): fit the intercept and slope above, apply them. Few parameters, robust, fixes the common patterns.
Isotonic regression: the CORP curve itself. Flexible, but needs plenty of data and produces step-shaped probabilities.

Fit the recalibration on data that wasn’t used to train the model, and evaluate on yet another set (scikit-learn: CalibratedClassifierCV). A monotone recalibration leaves the ranking, and therefore AUC and DSC, essentially unchanged. It only removes MCB.

title: Calibration and proper scoring rules
text:
Takeaways

Calibration asks whether predicted probabilities match observed frequencies. It’s separate from discrimination, and AUC can’t see it.
Prefer CORP reliability diagrams with consistency bands over binned diagrams. Bins and the ECE depend on arbitrary choices.
Calibration slope < 1 signals predictions that are too extreme (overfitting), > 1 too timid. The intercept shows systematic over- or under-prediction.
Compare models with proper scoring rules (log loss, Brier), and use the Murphy decomposition to see whether a difference comes from discrimination or calibration.
Check calibration within segments (A/E ratios). Overall calibration can hide large errors in the groups that matter.
